title: Drop-stitch lace
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 387. Public domain. The technique also appears in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s). Public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A deliberate wrap of the working yarn over the needle between stitches, creating a new loop and, in lace, an eyelet hole.

content.text: Drop-stitch lace works by dropping a yarn over off the needle on purpose. The dropped loop unravels down to the holding row below it. This makes a tall open column with no decrease needed. The stitch count stays correct because the yarn over was added first. The open column is the finished lace pattern.

You need yarn and needles. A smooth yarn in dk or aran weight makes the drop columns easiest to see and control. The yarn should have some elasticity so the dropped columns bloom open rather than collapsing.

attrs.title: Fig. 387, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
The following works a simple drop-stitch lace scarf pattern.
Cast on a multiple of 4 stitches, plus 2 for selvedge (e.g. 22 stitches).
Rows 1 to 3: knit across (garter stitch). These holding rows prevent the drop from travelling past this point.
Row 4 (drop row): k2, *yo twice, k2; repeat from * across. The double
yarn over
creates two extra loops on the right needle for each stitch position, inflating the row temporarily.

Row 5 (elongated row): k2, *drop the first yo loop off the needle (let it autumn), knit the second yo as a normal stitch, k2; repeat. The dropped yo unravels down to the holding rows, creating an open column. The remaining yo loop closes the stitch count back to normal.
Repeat rows 1 to 5 for the desired length. The garter-stitch holding rows and the drop rows alternate to produce the characteristic striped lace structure.
Where you'll see it

Drop-stitch lace is a common beginner lace technique because it requires only knit stitches and yarn overs with no paired decreases. It is widely used for scarves, shawls, and lightweight summer tops where open columns give a loose, drapey hand. It also appears as a decorative insert within an otherwise plain stocking-stitch fabric.
Common faults

Drop columns travelling too far. If holding rows are not worked at regular intervals, a dropped stitch will unravel all the way to the cast-on edge. Count the holding rows between each drop row and do not skip them.
Stitch count off after the drop row. Dropping both yarn overs rather than one leaves a hole and removes a stitch. Drop only the first yo of each double yo; the second becomes the working stitch.

Open columns closing up. If the yarn has no elasticity or is worked too tightly, the drop columns stay narrow rather than blooming. Block the finished piece by soaking and pinning the drop columns open while damp.
What to try next: once this feels comfortable, try eyelet lace. A
yarn over
paired with a decrease makes a small hole that stays put, rather than unravelling down the column.
